title: Could Rousseau make a comeback?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton revisits Rousseau, prompted by noticing that Rousseau valued good struggle in children's learning, a word absent from his own memory of the philosopher. He outlines Rousseau's developmental stages and practices such as guided freedom, learning through consequences and sensory experience before abstraction. He notes that schools which misapplied these ideas as unrigorous child-centred work helped provoke tighter national curricula. Prompted by reports of exam stress and a kindergarten graduation in caps and gowns, he argues schools have become managerial, results-driven and endless in assessment, forgetting that children are not small adults. He offers this as an admittedly unformed case for rereading Rousseau on age-appropriate development.
points: Rousseau's stages of development and his stress on experience, consequences and good struggle are summarised as a possible corrective to managerialised schooling.
Poor implementation of Rousseauian ideas in some schools undermined rigour and indirectly fed the push for prescriptive national curricula.
Treating young children as miniature adults, as in kindergarten graduations or heavy exam pressure, ignores that childhood differs by age.
Schools should aim for improvement that is appropriate to children's developmental stage rather than simply feeding exam reporting systems.
quotes: Rousseau’s big idea was that children were born largely in a ‘natural’ state but then grew up in a corrupt world. He was interested in what, if anything, could be done to hold off the corruption and allow children and young people to develop more ‘naturally’.

Reminding myself of what Rousseau thought made me begin to think that he might be due for a comeback. Not totally; that wouldn’t be possible. But he might have something to say to us about how the way so much of education and learning has been managerialised and may not be for the benefit of the learners.

Ironically, the failure in some schools to bring some of Rousseau’s ideas into fruition in a way that helped children and young people learn, was part of the stimulus that led to a tighter, more prescriptive national curriculum in the UK and elsewhere.

Does anyone believe that (except for the bit about a photo opportunity for parents)? It feels to me like an educational version of those horrific pageants in which young girls are made up to look like mini-adults and parade around in a beauty competition.

There are times when we seem to think that childhood doesn’t exist or that it doesn’t exist differently at different times. We put young people under stress as though they were mature adults; we dress them up and ask them to mimic an adulthood from which they are still a long way away.

On the other hand, it does feel to me that many schools have now become (have been encouraged to become) less about the learning and development of young children and more about results (which isn’t necessarily learning), about management, about endless assessment, about looking and behaving like conventional businesses.

We need to realise that those four and five year olds we are dressing up as ‘graduates’ have been on the earth for less than 1500 days. We need to remember that for most of that time, we are trying to support their development so that their learning can later take place enjoyably and beneficially.
